items.paragraph: Style manuals routinely tell writers to avoid the passive voice, and the advice has hardened into a rule that many writers apply without thinking. But the passive also does work that nothing else does as neatly. It lets a writer keep the topic of a paragraph in the subject position, so that a passage about a disease can go on talking about the disease ('it is spread by mosquitoes') rather than lurching to whatever happens to cause it. The useful question is never whether a sentence is passive but whether the reader needs to know who acted, and what the sentence should be about.

items.paragraph: Ask people why one accent sounds educated and another sounds careless, and they will usually point to the sounds themselves: clarity, crispness, a certain precision. (1) If refinement really lived in the sound, it would not change its value at a border. (2) What listeners hear as clarity is better understood as familiarity with the speech of people who already hold status, so that an accent gains prestige by association, much as an address or a school does. (3) None of this makes such judgements harmless. Because they feel like perceptions rather than prejudices, they are seldom examined, and a speaker can be passed over without anyone believing that the accent played any part. (4) The real difficulty is not that people defend accent hierarchies openly but that they rarely notice holding them at all.

options.A: Slang ages fast because it marks membership of a group, a role it loses once outsiders take it up; most terms then fade, though a few become ordinary words.
options.B: Slang words fade because advertisers and newsreaders deliberately adopt them in order to make young people abandon the private vocabulary of their group.
options.C: Slang is a poor and short-lived form of speech, and its rapid decline shows that it fails to communicate as clearly as the ordinary vocabulary of a language does.
options.D: Most of the ordinary words in a language began life as slang terms that young people once coined in order to mark themselves out as members of a particular group.

items.paragraph: Slang tends to age quickly, and the reason lies in what it is for. A slang word marks its users as insiders: to say it is to show that one belongs to a particular group, often a young one, and knows its current code. That function depends on outsiders not using the word. Once parents, advertisers and newsreaders adopt it, the word stops marking anyone as an insider, and the group that coined it drops it for something fresh. A few slang terms survive this process by losing their flavour entirely and becoming ordinary vocabulary, but most simply fade. The speed of slang's decline is, in this sense, a sign that it worked.

options.A: Recommendation systems serve users well by supplying more of what they already like, though people should still search elsewhere if they wish to broaden their tastes.
options.B: Because taste grows partly from exposure, systems that offer more of what people chose help fix and narrow their preferences, so they are not neutral mirrors.
options.C: Because people come to like what they meet repeatedly, recommendation systems are now the main force that decides which music, food and films people enjoy.
options.D: Recommendation systems deliberately manipulate users into liking content they would otherwise reject, and in doing so they deprive people of any real freedom of choice.

items.paragraph: Defenders of recommendation systems argue that they merely give people more of what they already like, and that this is a service rather than a manipulation. The claim assumes that preferences exist fully formed before the recommendations arrive. Taste, however, is partly made by exposure: people come to like music, food or films they have encountered repeatedly, and they rarely develop a liking for what they never meet. A system that learns from what someone has chosen, and then shows them more of the same, is therefore not simply reflecting a preference but helping to fix it, narrowing the range of encounters from which future preferences could grow. This need not be sinister, and the user remains free to search elsewhere. But it means the defence of such systems as neutral mirrors is mistaken.

items.paragraph: Almost every doctor and nurse knows that cleaning the hands before touching the next patient does more to stop hospital infections than almost any other single habit. Yet observations on busy wards repeatedly find that the step is skipped far more often than staff themselves believe. The gap is rarely a matter of ignorance or indifference. (1) On a crowded shift, a nurse may need to clean her hands dozens of times an hour, and each time the sink or dispenser is a few steps out of the way, the step competes with an alarm, a call or a patient in distress. (2) Campaigns that simply remind staff of the importance of hygiene therefore tend to produce short-lived improvements. options.A: An ending should be judged by its fit with the novel's concerns; an unresolved close can complete a book's argument, but openness adopted merely for effect is evasion.
options.B: Open endings are artistically superior to tidy ones, since resolving every question that a story raises insults the intelligence of its serious readers.
options.C: A novel about how difficult it is to know another person would contradict itself if its final chapter revealed everything about its characters' hidden inner lives and motives.
options.D: Readers who complain about unresolved endings are usually right, because a novel that withholds its answers has generally failed to finish what its early chapters began.

items.paragraph: Readers who complain that a novel simply stops often assume that an ending exists to settle what the story has raised: who is guilty, who marries whom, whether the journey succeeds. Some endings do that, and do it well. But an ending can also be judged by whether it completes the shape of the book's attention. A novel that has spent three hundred pages showing how hard it is to know another person would contradict itself if its last chapter revealed everything; the unresolved close is then not a failure of nerve but the argument carried through. Openness is not a virtue in itself, and a writer who withholds an answer merely to seem profound has evaded rather than completed the work. The question is not whether an ending is closed but whether it is faithful to what the novel has been about.
